en.title: Anatomy: the whole course
en.short: What anatomy covers, how anatomy degrees and courses are organised, and how to study the subject well.

sections.heading: Read this first
sections.text:
These notes teach anatomy as a subject. They are not medical advice, and they do not replace your teachers, textbooks, laboratory sessions or official guidance. They give no drug doses. Clinical rules change and differ between countries, so check the current national or World Health Organization (WHO) guidance when a clinical point arises.

Anatomy also involves human material, images and body donation. Treat donors, images and classmates with respect. Follow your institution’s rules on consent, photography and laboratory conduct.

sections.heading: What anatomy is
sections.text:
Anatomy is the study of the structure of the body. It asks what parts exist, where they lie, how they relate to one another, and how structure supports function. Gross anatomy studies parts you can see with the naked eye. Histology studies tissues under the microscope. Embryology studies development before birth. Neuroanatomy studies the brain, spinal cord and nerves.

Anatomy uses a shared language. Terms such as anterior, posterior, medial, lateral, proximal and distal describe position. Planes such as sagittal, coronal and transverse describe sections. Learning this language early makes everything else easier.

sections.heading: How the degree is organised
sections.text:
Length, awards and course structure differ by country and institution, so check your own handbook. In Nigeria, anatomy is often offered as a BSc degree, commonly over four years, with later MSc and PhD study. Medical, nursing and allied health students usually take anatomy in their early years.

In the United Kingdom, anatomy is usually integrated into medical degrees rather than taught as a separate degree, though some universities offer related BSc programmes. In the United States, many students study anatomy in medical school after a first degree. Some schools teach by body region; others teach by system. The content is similar.

sections.heading: The main areas in teaching order
sections.text:
Courses usually begin with terminology and the body plan, then cells, basic tissues and histology. Embryology explains how structures form. The skeletal and muscular systems introduce support and movement. The cardiovascular, respiratory, digestive, urinary and reproductive systems follow.

The core stage is regional. Students study the upper limb, lower limb, thorax and mediastinum, abdomen and peritoneum, pelvis and perineum, and head and neck. Neuroanatomy, cranial nerves, the autonomic nervous system and special senses come alongside. Endocrine, lymphatic, immune and integumentary anatomy complete the systems.

Later topics connect anatomy to practice: radiological and sectional anatomy, surface anatomy and clinical examination, and ethics of body donation. Master’s level work adds advanced neuroanatomy, advanced developmental anatomy, research methods, and computational and imaging anatomy.

sections.heading: How to study anatomy
sections.text:
Use active recall rather than only rereading. Draw structures from memory, label blank diagrams, and explain a region aloud without notes. Space your revision over weeks. Mix old and new topics in each session.

Learn in three dimensions. Use models, prosections, dissection videos and radiological images. Trace a structure from origin to ending, and ask what lies beside it. Link each fact to function and to a simple clinical example, such as why a nerve injury weakens a particular muscle.

Work in small groups to test one another. Keep a personal list of terms you confuse. Visit the laboratory regularly, and ask staff when a relationship is unclear.

sections.heading: Common mistakes
sections.text:
Students often memorise lists without building a mental picture, so they cannot find a structure in a specimen or scan. Others ignore embryology, then struggle with birth defects and adult arrangements. Confusing left and right, or using terms loosely, causes errors in examinations and later practice.

Some students skip histology because it seems separate, but tissues explain how organs work. Others rely on one textbook or on social media summaries without checking a standard source. Finally, do not use anatomy notes to diagnose yourself or others. Clinical decisions need a qualified clinician who can assess the person directly.

keyPoints: Anatomy studies body structure and the relationships between parts.
A shared terminology of position, planes and movement is the foundation.
Courses usually move from tissues and development to systems, then regions.
Learn in three dimensions using models, images and laboratory material.
Active recall and spaced revision work better than rereading.
These notes teach concepts and are not medical advice.

en.title: Anatomical terminology and the body plan
en.short: The language of anatomy: position, planes, directional terms, regions, cavities, movements and imaging orientation.

sections.heading: Position and planes
sections.text: Anatomical position is standing upright, head and eyes forward, arms at the sides, palms forward, feet together. All descriptions assume it. A plane divides the body. The median or midsagittal plane runs vertically through the midline into equal right and left halves. A sagittal plane is parallel to it. The coronal or frontal plane divides front from back. The transverse or axial plane divides upper from lower.

sections.heading: Directional terms
sections.text: Directional terms describe one part relative to another. Superior means nearer the head, inferior nearer the feet. Anterior means nearer the front, posterior nearer the back. Medial means nearer the midline, lateral farther from it. Proximal means nearer the trunk or origin, distal farther away. Superficial means nearer the surface, deep farther in. Ipsilateral means same side, contralateral opposite side. The elbow is proximal to the wrist, distal to the shoulder.

sections.heading: Regions and cavities
sections.text: Body regions include the head, neck, trunk, and upper and lower limbs. The trunk has thoracic, abdominal and pelvic parts. The two main cavities are ventral and dorsal. The ventral cavity contains the thoracic cavity, with the lungs and heart, and the abdominopelvic cavity. The dorsal cavity contains the cranial cavity, holding the brain, and the vertebral canal, holding the spinal cord. The diaphragm separates thoracic from abdominal cavities.

sections.heading: Movement and imaging
sections.text:
Movement terms describe change at a joint. Flexion decreases the angle, extension increases it. Abduction moves a limb away from the midline, adduction towards it. Rotation turns a bone around its axis. Pronation turns the palm down, supination up. Inversion turns the sole inward, eversion outward. Dorsiflexion lifts the foot, plantarflexion points it down. Circumduction is circular movement.

On axial computed tomography (CT) and MRI scans, images are viewed from the feet upward, so the patient’s right appears on the viewer’s left. Coronal images are viewed from the front. For example, a shadow in the right upper abdomen must be described with its plane and side, because left and right are reversed on axial images.

keyPoints: Anatomical position is the reference for all descriptions: upright, palms forward.
Median, coronal and transverse planes divide the body in three standard ways.
Superior, inferior, anterior, posterior, medial, lateral, proximal and distal are relative terms.
Ventral and dorsal cavities contain the thoracic, abdominopelvic, cranial and vertebral spaces.
Flexion, extension, abduction, adduction, rotation, pronation and supination name joint movements.
On axial images the patient’s right appears on the viewer’s left, so check orientation labels.

en.title: Cells, basic tissues and histology
en.short: Cell structure, the four basic tissues, epithelial types, connective, muscle, nerve, microscopy and staining.

sections.heading: Cell structure
sections.text: A cell is the smallest living unit. The plasma membrane controls what enters and leaves. The nucleus holds DNA and directs protein synthesis. Cytoplasm contains organelles: mitochondria make ATP, ribosomes build proteins, endoplasmic reticulum folds and transports them, and the Golgi apparatus packages them. Lysosomes digest waste. Structure matches function: cells that secrete protein, such as pancreatic acinar cells, have abundant rough endoplasmic reticulum, while muscle cells have many mitochondria for contraction.

sections.heading: Four basic tissues
sections.text: Histology is the study of tissue structure, usually with a microscope. The four basic tissues are epithelial, connective, muscle and nervous. Epithelium covers surfaces, lines cavities and forms glands. Connective tissue supports, binds, stores and transports. Muscle contracts. Nervous tissue conducts electrical signals. Organs combine these tissues; for example, the small intestine has epithelium for absorption, connective tissue in its wall, smooth muscle for movement and nerves for control.

sections.heading: Epithelium and connective
sections.text: Epithelia are classified by cell shape and number of layers. Simple squamous epithelium is thin for exchange, as in lung alveoli. Simple cuboidal and columnar epithelia line ducts and absorb or secrete. Stratified squamous epithelium resists wear, as in the mouth and skin. Pseudostratified epithelium, a single layer of cells that looks layered, lines the airways. Connective tissue has cells, fibres and ground substance, the gel-like material between the cells. Loose connective tissue cushions; dense regular connective tissue forms tendons and ligaments; cartilage and bone are firm connective tissues; blood is a fluid connective tissue.

sections.heading: Muscle, nerve, microscopy
sections.text: Muscle is skeletal, cardiac or smooth. Skeletal muscle is striated and voluntary; cardiac muscle is striated and involuntary; smooth muscle is non-striated and involuntary. Nervous tissue contains neurons, which carry impulses, and neuroglia, which support them. For microscopy, tissue is fixed, sectioned and stained. Haematoxylin and eosin (H&E) is common: haematoxylin stains nuclei blue-purple and eosin stains cytoplasm pink. Total magnification equals eyepiece magnification times objective magnification. A 10× eyepiece with a 40× objective gives 400×.

keyPoints: Histology studies tissues; the four basic tissues are epithelial, connective, muscle and nervous.
Epithelium is classified by cell shape and number of layers, and its structure suits its function.
Connective tissue has cells, fibres and ground substance and includes loose, dense, cartilage, bone and blood.
Skeletal and cardiac muscle are striated; smooth muscle is not striated.
Neurons conduct impulses and neuroglia support them.
Total magnification = eyepiece magnification × objective magnification; H&E stains nuclei blue-purple and cytoplasm pink.

en.title: Embryology and human development
en.short: From fertilisation to birth: germ layers, folding, organogenesis, placenta and congenital anomalies.

sections.heading: Fertilisation to implantation
sections.text: Fertilisation is the fusion of a sperm and an oocyte, usually in the ampulla of the uterine tube. It restores the diploid chromosome number and starts cleavage: rapid mitotic divisions without much growth. The cluster becomes a morula, then a blastocyst with an inner cell mass and an outer trophoblast. Implantation is the attachment and embedding of the blastocyst in the endometrium, beginning about six days after fertilisation. The trophoblast helps form the placenta.

sections.heading: Gastrulation and folding
sections.text: Gastrulation, in the third week, rearranges the bilaminar (two-layered) disc into three germ layers. The ectoderm forms the epidermis of the skin and nervous tissue; the mesoderm forms muscle, bone, blood and much of the urogenital system; the endoderm lines the gut and gives rise to associated organs. Folding then turns the flat disc into a three-dimensional tube. Craniocaudal folding forms head and tail folds, and lateral folding brings the body walls together around the gut.

sections.heading: Organogenesis, arches and limbs
sections.text: Organogenesis is the formation of organs, mainly during the embryonic period, about weeks 3 to 8. The pharyngeal arches are paired bars of tissue in the future head and neck. They contribute to the face, jaw, middle ear bones, laryngeal cartilages and some muscles and nerves. Limb development begins with limb buds; the apical ectodermal ridge guides outgrowth, and programmed cell death separates the digits. Defects in these processes cause anomalies such as cleft lip or polydactyly.

sections.heading: Membranes, placenta and anomalies
sections.text: The fetal membranes are the amnion, chorion, yolk sac and allantois. The placenta develops from chorionic villi and maternal decidua (the modified endometrial lining). It exchanges gases, nutrients and waste and makes hormones, but it is not a complete barrier. Teratogens are agents that cause congenital anomalies, which are defects present at birth. Timing matters: the embryonic period is most sensitive. For example, rubella in early pregnancy can damage the eyes, ears and heart. Prevention advice varies, so check current national or WHO guidance.

keyPoints: Fertilisation usually occurs in the ampulla of the uterine tube and is followed by cleavage and blastocyst formation.
Implantation embeds the blastocyst in the endometrium.
Gastrulation forms ectoderm, mesoderm and endoderm; folding makes the embryo tubular.
Organogenesis occurs mainly in weeks 3 to 8, and pharyngeal arches and limb buds form during this period.
The placenta exchanges substances and makes hormones but does not block all teratogens.
Teratogen effects depend on timing, and congenital anomalies are defects present at birth.

en.title: Skeletal system: bone and joints
en.short: Bone structure, ossification, growth, remodelling, axial and appendicular skeleton, joint types and movements.

sections.heading: Bone structure
sections.text:
Bone is living tissue. Its matrix is collagen, which gives flexibility, and mineral salts, mainly calcium phosphate in hydroxyapatite, which give hardness. Compact bone is dense and forms the outer shell. Spongy bone is a network of trabeculae, small struts that resist stress.

A long bone has a diaphysis (shaft), epiphyses (ends) and marrow. The periosteum is a fibrous covering with blood vessels and osteoblasts, bone-forming cells. Osteocytes are mature bone cells in lacunae. Osteoclasts resorb bone. An osteon is the unit of compact bone: lamellae around a central canal.

sections.heading: Ossification and growth
sections.text:
Ossification is the formation of bone. In intramembranous ossification, mesenchyme becomes bone directly; this forms flat skull bones and the clavicle. In endochondral ossification, a cartilage model is replaced by bone; this forms most long bones. Primary centres appear in the diaphysis and secondary centres in the epiphyses.

Growth in length occurs at the epiphyseal plate until it closes. Growth in width is appositional, by new bone under the periosteum. Remodelling is continuous resorption by osteoclasts and deposition by osteoblasts. It repairs microdamage and adjusts bone to load, as Wolff’s law describes.

sections.heading: Skeleton and joints
sections.text:
The axial skeleton is the skull, vertebral column, ribs and sternum; it supports the head, neck and trunk. The appendicular skeleton is the limbs and their girdles; it allows movement.

Joints are classified by tissue. Fibrous joints have dense connective tissue and little movement, as between skull bones. Cartilaginous joints have cartilage, as between vertebrae, and allow slight movement. Synovial joints have a fluid-filled cavity and are freely movable.

sections.heading: Synovial joints
sections.text:
A synovial joint has articular cartilage, a joint capsule with fibrous and synovial layers, and synovial fluid for lubrication and nutrition. Ligaments, menisci and bursae may add stability or reduce friction. Movements include flexion, extension, abduction, adduction, rotation and circumduction.

Chidi fractures his radius in a bicycle fall: the radius is appendicular, and his elbow is a synovial hinge joint allowing flexion and extension.

keyPoints: Bone matrix combines collagen for flexibility with hydroxyapatite mineral for hardness.
Compact bone is organised into osteons; spongy bone is a trabecular network.
Intramembranous ossification forms flat skull bones; endochondral ossification forms most long bones.
Longitudinal growth occurs at the epiphyseal plate; width grows by apposition under the periosteum.
The axial skeleton supports the trunk; the appendicular skeleton includes limbs and girdles.
Synovial joints have a capsule and synovial fluid and allow movements such as flexion and rotation.

en.title: Muscular system
en.short: Skeletal, smooth and cardiac muscle; organisation, attachments, fascia, compartments, tendons and innervation.

sections.heading: Three muscle types
sections.text: Muscle tissue produces force by shortening. Skeletal muscle is voluntary and striated, meaning it has a striped appearance. It has long, multinucleated fibres and moves the skeleton. Smooth muscle is involuntary and non-striated. It lies in the walls of hollow organs and blood vessels, such as the gut and uterus, and moves contents or changes vessel width. Cardiac muscle is involuntary and striated. Its branched cells join at intercalated discs, which help electrical signals spread through the heart. It forms the wall of the heart.

sections.heading: Skeletal muscle organisation
sections.text: A skeletal muscle is arranged in bundles. The whole muscle is covered by epimysium. Bundles called fascicles are wrapped by perimysium, and each muscle fibre by endomysium. Inside a fibre, myofibrils are divided into sarcomeres, the units that shorten. A tendon is dense connective tissue that attaches muscle to bone. A flat tendon is an aponeurosis. The origin is the attachment that is usually fixed, often proximal. The insertion is the attachment that usually moves, often distal. The action is the movement produced, such as flexion. In the arm, biceps brachii arises from the scapula, inserts on the radius, and flexes the elbow and supinates the forearm, turning the palm upward. Its nerve is the musculocutaneous nerve.

sections.heading: Fascia and compartments
sections.text: Fascia is connective tissue that surrounds muscles, vessels and nerves. Superficial fascia lies under the skin. Deep fascia forms sheets and holds muscles in place. In the limbs, deep fascia and bone enclose compartments. Each compartment contains muscles that often share an action and a nerve. For example, the anterior compartment of the arm contains the elbow flexors, supplied mainly by the musculocutaneous nerve. Swelling inside a closed compartment can raise pressure and harm nerves and vessels, so doctors watch for compartment syndrome. Innervation means the nerve supply. Somatic motor nerves tell skeletal muscle fibres to contract at the neuromuscular junction. One motor neuron and the fibres it supplies form a motor unit. Sensory nerves also report position and movement.

keyPoints: Skeletal muscle is voluntary and striated, smooth muscle is involuntary and non-striated, and cardiac muscle is involuntary, striated and joined by intercalated discs.
Skeletal muscle is organised into fascicles, with epimysium around the muscle, perimysium around fascicles and endomysium around fibres.
The origin is usually the fixed attachment, the insertion usually moves, and the action is the movement produced.
Tendons attach muscle to bone, and aponeuroses are broad flat tendons.
Deep fascia helps enclose limb compartments, whose muscles often share a nerve and an action.
Somatic motor neurons innervate skeletal muscle at neuromuscular junctions, and a motor unit is one motor neuron plus the fibres it supplies.

en.title: Cardiovascular system: heart and circulation
en.short: Heart chambers, valves, pericardium, coronary and conduction systems, great vessels, and fetal circulation.

sections.heading: Chambers and valves
sections.text: The heart has four chambers. The right atrium receives deoxygenated blood through the venae cavae. The right ventricle pumps it through the pulmonary trunk to the lungs. The left atrium receives oxygenated blood through the pulmonary veins. The left ventricle pumps it into the aorta. Valves prevent backflow. The tricuspid and mitral valves sit between atria and ventricles. The pulmonary and aortic valves sit at ventricular exits.

sections.heading: Pericardium and coronary
sections.text: The pericardium is the sac around the heart. Its fibrous layer is tough; its serous layer has parietal and visceral parts. The visceral part is the epicardium. The pericardial cavity holds fluid that reduces friction. The coronary arteries supply the heart muscle. The right and left coronary arteries arise above the aortic valve. Cardiac veins drain into the coronary sinus and the right atrium. Blockage can cause angina or infarction.

sections.heading: Conduction and vessels
sections.text: The conduction system sets the rhythm. The sinoatrial node in the right atrium starts each beat. The atrioventricular node delays the signal. The bundle of His carries it down the interventricular septum. Bundle branches and Purkinje fibres spread it to ventricular muscle. The great vessels are the aorta, pulmonary trunk, superior and inferior venae cavae, and pulmonary veins. The aorta carries oxygenated blood to the body. The pulmonary trunk carries deoxygenated blood to the lungs.

sections.heading: Circulations and fetus
sections.text: Pulmonary circulation goes from right ventricle to lungs and back to left atrium. Systemic circulation goes from left ventricle to body and back to right atrium. In the fetus, the placenta exchanges gases, not the lungs. The umbilical vein carries oxygenated blood to the fetus. The ductus venosus bypasses the liver. The foramen ovale passes blood from right atrium to left atrium. The ductus arteriosus passes blood from pulmonary trunk to aorta. Umbilical arteries carry deoxygenated blood to the placenta. Shunts close after birth. For example, Amina, a newborn in Kano, with a patent ductus arteriosus has extra blood from aorta to pulmonary artery, raising lung blood flow.

keyPoints: Blood flows from right atrium to right ventricle to lungs to left atrium to left ventricle to aorta.
Valves prevent backflow: tricuspid and mitral between atria and ventricles, pulmonary and aortic at ventricular exits.
The pericardium is a fibrous and serous sac; the coronary arteries arise above the aortic valve and veins drain to the coronary sinus.
The sinoatrial node starts the beat; the atrioventricular node delays it before the bundle of His and Purkinje fibres spread it.
Pulmonary circulation carries deoxygenated blood to the lungs; systemic circulation carries oxygenated blood to the body.
In fetal circulation the placenta exchanges gases, and the ductus venosus, foramen ovale and ductus arteriosus are shunts that close after birth.

en.title: Respiratory system
en.short: Upper and lower airways, larynx, trachea, bronchi, lungs, pleura and the muscles of breathing.

sections.heading: Upper tract and larynx
sections.text: The upper respiratory tract is the nose, nasal cavity, paranasal sinuses and pharynx; many texts include the larynx. Clinically, the vocal cords mark the boundary. The nose warms, moistens and filters air. The pharynx is a shared air and food passage. The larynx is a cartilage box containing the vocal folds. It protects the airway during swallowing, produces voice and helps coughing. Its main cartilages are thyroid, cricoid, epiglottis and paired arytenoids.

sections.heading: Trachea and bronchi
sections.text: The lower respiratory tract is the trachea, bronchi and lungs. The trachea runs from the larynx to the sternal angle, where it divides at the carina into right and left main bronchi. Hyaline cartilage rings keep it open; trachealis muscle fills the posterior gap. The right main bronchus is wider, shorter and more vertical, so inhaled objects more often enter it. Each main bronchus divides into lobar bronchi, then segmental bronchi. A bronchopulmonary segment is a lung unit with its own segmental bronchus and artery.

sections.heading: Lungs and pleura
sections.text: The right lung has three lobes and the left has two, with the lingula on the left. The hilum contains the main bronchus, pulmonary vessels, nerves and lymphatics. Each lung is covered by visceral pleura; parietal pleura lines the chest wall, diaphragm and mediastinum. Between them is the pleural cavity, a film of serous fluid that lets surfaces slide. Surface tension helps hold the lung against the chest wall.

sections.heading: Diaphragm and ventilation
sections.text: The diaphragm is dome-shaped. The phrenic nerve, from spinal roots C3 to C5, supplies it. Its openings transmit the inferior vena cava at T8, oesophagus at T10 and aorta at T12. Quiet inspiration is diaphragmatic: contraction flattens the dome and lowers thoracic pressure. External intercostals lift the ribs. Forced inspiration uses scalenes and sternocleidomastoid. Quiet expiration is passive; forced expiration uses internal intercostals and abdominal muscles. An inhaled peanut more often enters the right main bronchus.

keyPoints: The upper respiratory tract includes the nose, pharynx and usually the larynx; the lower tract is the trachea, bronchi and lungs.
The larynx protects the airway and produces voice using the vocal folds.
The right main bronchus is wider, shorter and more vertical, so inhaled objects more often enter it.
The right lung has three lobes and the left has two; the pleura is a double membrane with serous fluid between its layers.
The diaphragm is the main muscle of quiet inspiration and is supplied by the phrenic nerve from C3 to C5.
Forced inspiration uses accessory muscles, while forced expiration uses internal intercostals and abdominal muscles.

en.title: Digestive system: tract, accessory organs and portal circulation
en.short: This summary covers the gut tube from mouth to anus, accessory organs, peritoneum, mesenteries and portal blood supply.

sections.heading: Gut tube
sections.text:
The digestive tract runs from the oral cavity to the anal canal. Teeth and tongue break up food; saliva moistens it. The pharynx and oesophagus conduct food by peristalsis, waves of muscle contraction. The stomach stores food, secretes acid and pepsin, and forms chyme.

The small intestine has duodenum, jejunum and ileum; most digestion and absorption occur here. The large intestine absorbs water and electrolytes and forms faeces. The rectum stores faeces; the anal canal opens to the exterior, guarded by sphincters.

sections.heading: Accessory organs
sections.text:
Accessory organs aid digestion. Salivary glands make saliva. The liver makes bile, processes nutrients and detoxifies blood. The gallbladder stores and concentrates bile. The pancreas releases digestive enzymes into the duodenum and hormones such as insulin into blood.

The duodenum receives bile and pancreatic juice through the major duodenal papilla. Bile emulsifies fat; enzymes break down proteins, fats and carbohydrates.

sections.heading: Peritoneum and mesenteries
sections.text:
The peritoneum is a serous membrane. Parietal peritoneum lines the abdominal wall; visceral peritoneum covers organs. The peritoneal cavity holds a thin film of fluid.

Intraperitoneal organs are suspended by mesentery, a double layer of peritoneum carrying vessels and nerves. Retroperitoneal organs lie behind the peritoneum, such as the kidneys, pancreas, most of the duodenum, and the ascending and descending colon. Mesenteries include the small intestine mesentery and transverse mesocolon.

sections.heading: Blood supply and portal system
sections.text:
Arterial supply follows gut regions. The foregut, to the major duodenal papilla, is supplied by the coeliac trunk. The midgut, to two-thirds along the transverse colon, is supplied by the superior mesenteric artery. The hindgut, to the upper anal canal, is supplied by the inferior mesenteric artery.

Venous blood drains to the portal vein, formed by superior mesenteric and splenic veins, then through liver sinusoids to hepatic veins and inferior vena cava. Case: Amina swallows a maize grain. It passes mouth, oesophagus, stomach, small intestine, colon, rectum, anal canal. Most nutrients absorbed in the small intestine enter portal blood and reach the liver first; fats travel in lymph instead.

keyPoints: The digestive tract runs from the oral cavity to the anal canal, and the small intestine is the main site of digestion and absorption.
Accessory organs are the salivary glands, liver, gallbladder and pancreas; bile and pancreatic juice enter the duodenum.
The peritoneum has parietal and visceral layers; mesentery is a double layer that suspends intraperitoneal organs and carries vessels.
Retroperitoneal organs include the kidneys, pancreas, most of the duodenum, and the ascending and descending colon.
The foregut, midgut and hindgut are supplied by the coeliac trunk, superior mesenteric artery and inferior mesenteric artery.
Gut venous blood drains by the portal vein to liver sinusoids before reaching the inferior vena cava.

en.title: Urinary and reproductive systems
en.short: Kidneys, urinary tract, male and female reproductive organs, perineum, pelvic floor and mammary glands.

sections.heading: Kidneys and urine flow
sections.text: The kidneys are paired retroperitoneal organs that filter blood and make urine. Each kidney has about one million nephrons, its functional units. A nephron begins with a glomerulus, where plasma is filtered, then a tubule that reabsorbs useful substances and secretes waste. The kidneys also help control fluid, electrolytes, acid-base balance and blood pressure. Urine drains from the renal pelvis into a ureter, a muscular tube that moves urine by peristalsis to the bladder. The ureter enters the bladder obliquely, helping prevent backflow.

sections.heading: Bladder and urethra
sections.text: The bladder is a hollow muscular organ. Its detrusor muscle contracts to empty urine. The internal urethral sphincter is smooth muscle and involuntary; the external sphincter is skeletal muscle and voluntary. The urethra carries urine out. In males it is long, passes through the prostate and also carries semen. In females it is short and opens in front of the vagina. This shorter urethra helps explain why urinary infection is more common in women; diagnosis and treatment follow current local guidance.

sections.heading: Reproductive organs
sections.text: Male reproductive organs include the testes, epididymides, vas deferens, seminal vesicles, prostate, bulbourethral glands and penis. The testes make sperm and testosterone. The epididymis stores and matures sperm, and the vas deferens carries them. The glands add fluid to form semen. Female organs include the ovaries, uterine tubes, uterus, cervix and vagina. The ovaries make oocytes and hormones. Fertilisation usually occurs in a uterine tube. The uterus wall has an endometrium, myometrium and perimetrium, and the cervix is its lower part. The vulva is the external genital region.

sections.heading: Pelvic floor and breasts
sections.text: The perineum is the region below the pelvic floor, around the external genitalia and anus. The pelvic floor, or pelvic diaphragm, is a muscular sheet supporting pelvic organs and helping control urine and faeces. Mammary glands are modified sweat glands in the breasts. Lobules make milk, and ducts carry it to the nipple. A teaching case: weakened pelvic floor after childbirth can cause urine leakage on coughing; anatomy explains support, and care follows local guidance.

keyPoints: The kidney nephron filters plasma, then the tubule reabsorbs and secretes.
Ureters move urine by peristalsis and enter the bladder obliquely to prevent backflow.
The bladder stores urine; the internal sphincter is involuntary and the external sphincter is voluntary.
The male urethra is long and shared with semen; the female urethra is short and separate from the reproductive tract.
Testes make sperm and testosterone; ovaries make oocytes and hormones; fertilisation usually occurs in a uterine tube.
The pelvic floor supports pelvic organs and helps continence; mammary glands are modified sweat glands.

en.title: Nervous system: foundations
en.short: Covers neurons, grey and white matter, brain regions, spinal cord, meninges, ventricles, CSF and basic pathways.

sections.heading: Neurons and matter
sections.text: A neuron receives, integrates and transmits information. Its cell body holds the nucleus; dendrites receive signals; an axon carries signals away; synapses pass them on. Sensory neurons bring information in, motor neurons send commands out, and interneurons connect them. Grey matter contains cell bodies, dendrites and synapses. White matter contains myelinated axons. In the brain, grey matter lies in the cortex and deep nuclei (clusters of cell bodies), with white matter beneath. In the spinal cord, grey matter is central and white matter outside.

sections.heading: Brain and cord
sections.text: The cerebrum handles conscious sensation, movement, thought and memory. The cerebellum coordinates movement and balance. The brainstem, made of midbrain, pons and medulla, links brain and spinal cord and controls vital functions. The spinal cord is a column of nervous tissue inside the vertebral canal. It carries ascending sensory tracts (bundles of axons) to the brain and descending motor tracts from it, and organises reflexes. A reflex arc uses a sensory neuron and a motor neuron, often with an interneuron between them, allowing response without conscious thought.

sections.heading: Meninges and CSF
sections.text: Three meninges cover the central nervous system: dura mater, arachnoid mater and pia mater. The dura is tough; the arachnoid is middle; the pia lies on the surface. Cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) fills the ventricles and subarachnoid space. The ventricles are four connected cavities: two lateral, the third and the fourth. Choroid plexus makes CSF. It flows lateral to third to fourth ventricle, then into the subarachnoid space, and is absorbed into dural venous sinuses through arachnoid granulations. CSF cushions the brain and helps remove waste.

sections.heading: Pathways and case
sections.text: Basic pathways are routes for information. Ascending pathways carry sensation upward; descending pathways carry motor commands downward. Many cross the midline, so one side of the brain controls the opposite side of the body. Case: Amina, after a road crash, has a spinal cord injury at T4, a chest-level segment. The cord carries ascending and descending signals, so she loses some sensation and movement below that level. Blocked CSF can raise pressure and harm brain tissue.

keyPoints: Neurons receive, integrate and transmit signals; sensory neurons bring information in, motor neurons send commands out, and interneurons connect them.
Grey matter contains cell bodies and synapses; white matter contains myelinated axons.
In the brain, grey matter is in the cortex and deep nuclei; in the spinal cord, grey matter is central.
The cerebrum, cerebellum and brainstem are major brain regions; the spinal cord carries tracts and organises reflexes.
The meninges are dura mater, arachnoid mater and pia mater; CSF is made by choroid plexus and absorbed by arachnoid granulations.
Ascending pathways carry sensation and descending pathways carry motor commands; many cross the midline, and reflex arcs allow rapid responses.

en.title: Upper limb anatomy
en.short: Bones, joints, muscles, nerves, vessels and clinical anatomy of the upper limb.

sections.heading: Bones and joints
sections.text:
The upper limb attaches to the trunk at the sternoclavicular joint, the only synovial link to the axial skeleton. Clavicle and scapula form the pectoral girdle. The humerus meets the scapula at the glenohumeral joint, a shallow ball-and-socket joint.

The elbow is a hinge between humerus and ulna; the radius allows pronation and supination at the radioulnar joints. The wrist is a condyloid joint between radius and carpal bones, with an ulnar disc. Carpals, metacarpals and phalanges form the hand.

sections.heading: Muscles and compartments
sections.text:
Fascia divides the arm and forearm into compartments. The arm’s anterior compartment contains biceps brachii, brachialis and coracobrachialis, supplied by musculocutaneous nerve; the posterior contains triceps brachii, supplied by radial nerve.

Forearm anterior muscles mainly flex the wrist and fingers; posterior muscles mainly extend them. The hand has thenar, hypothenar and central compartments plus interossei. Compartment syndrome is raised pressure within a closed fascial space, threatening nerves and muscles.

sections.heading: Nerves and vessels
sections.text:
The brachial plexus arises from ventral rami of C5 to T1 and passes through roots, trunks, divisions, cords and terminal branches. Its main terminal branches are musculocutaneous, axillary, radial, median and ulnar nerves.

The axillary artery becomes the brachial artery at the lower border of teres major; the brachial artery divides into radial and ulnar arteries in the cubital fossa. These form the palmar arches. Superficial lymphatics drain mainly to axillary nodes, some to cubital nodes; deep lymphatics follow vessels.

sections.heading: Surface and clinical
sections.text:
Surface landmarks include the deltoid, biceps, cubital fossa, radial pulse lateral to flexor carpi radialis, and anatomical snuffbox. Common correlations: clavicle fracture; anterior shoulder dislocation, risking axillary nerve; humeral shaft fracture, risking radial nerve; supracondylar fracture, risking brachial artery and median nerve; scaphoid fracture, risking avascular necrosis; carpal tunnel syndrome, compressing median nerve.

Example: a student falls on an outstretched hand and has snuffbox tenderness. Scaphoid fracture is suspected; its blood supply enters distally, so a proximal fragment may die. Imaging and orthopaedic referral are needed.

keyPoints: The sternoclavicular joint is the only synovial link between the upper limb and axial skeleton.
The glenohumeral joint is shallow and mobile, while the elbow is a stable hinge.
Arm and forearm muscles are grouped into fascial compartments with characteristic nerve supply.
The brachial plexus runs from roots C5 to T1 through trunks, divisions and cords to five terminal branches.
The axillary artery becomes the brachial artery at teres major and divides into radial and ulnar arteries in the cubital fossa.
Common fracture and compression patterns follow nerve and vessel anatomy, such as radial nerve at the humeral shaft and median nerve at the carpal tunnel.

en.title: Lower limb anatomy
en.short: Bones, joints, compartments, nerves, vessels, lymphatics and clinical links of the lower limb.

sections.heading: Bones and joints
sections.text: The lower limb skeleton is the femur, patella, tibia, fibula, tarsals, metatarsals and phalanges. The hip is a synovial ball and socket joint between the acetabulum and femoral head. The knee is a modified hinge joint with menisci, cruciate ligaments and collateral ligaments. The ankle is a hinge between the talus and the tibia and fibula. The subtalar joint allows inversion and eversion.

sections.heading: Compartments and nerves
sections.text: The thigh has anterior, medial and posterior compartments. The anterior compartment contains quadriceps, supplied by the femoral nerve from the lumbar plexus (L1 to L4). The medial compartment contains adductors, supplied by the obturator nerve. The posterior compartment contains hamstrings, supplied by the sciatic nerve from the sacral plexus (L4 to S4). The leg has anterior, lateral and posterior compartments. The anterior compartment is supplied by the deep fibular nerve, the lateral by the superficial fibular nerve, and the posterior by the tibial nerve. The sciatic nerve divides into tibial and common fibular nerves.

sections.heading: Vessels and lymphatics
sections.text: The femoral artery is the main supply. It becomes the popliteal artery behind the knee. The popliteal gives the anterior tibial artery and the posterior tibial artery; the fibular artery arises from the posterior tibial. The great saphenous vein runs medially to the femoral vein; the small saphenous vein runs posteriorly to the popliteal vein. Superficial inguinal nodes drain most of the limb. Popliteal nodes drain the lateral foot and posterolateral leg. Deep inguinal nodes accompany the femoral vessels.

sections.heading: Landmarks and clinical links
sections.text: Surface landmarks include the inguinal ligament, femoral triangle, adductor canal, popliteal fossa, patella, tibial tuberosity, malleoli, Achilles tendon and dorsalis pedis pulse. Common correlations are hip fracture, knee ligament or meniscal injury, ankle sprain, deep vein thrombosis, sciatica and compartment syndrome. In a case, Chidi falls from a motorcycle and has a tense, painful calf with severe pain on passive toe stretch. This suggests compartment syndrome, which needs urgent surgical assessment; foot pulses may remain present.

keyPoints: Lumbar plexus (L1 to L4) supplies the anterior and medial thigh; sacral plexus (L4 to S4) supplies the posterior thigh, leg and foot.
Thigh compartments: anterior femoral, medial obturator, posterior sciatic; leg compartments: anterior deep fibular, lateral superficial fibular, posterior tibial.
The femoral artery becomes popliteal and then tibial and fibular arteries; saphenous veins are superficial.
Superficial inguinal nodes drain most of the lower limb; popliteal nodes drain the lateral foot and posterolateral leg.
Pain out of proportion and pain on passive stretch suggest compartment syndrome, a surgical emergency.
Surface landmarks guide pulses, joint examination and safe procedures.

en.title: Thorax and mediastinum
en.short: Thoracic wall, ribs, intercostal spaces, mediastinal divisions and diaphragmatic openings for imaging and procedures.

sections.heading: Thoracic wall and ribs
sections.text: The thoracic wall is the bony and muscular cage around the lungs and heart. It has 12 pairs of ribs. Typical ribs 3 to 9 have a head, neck, tubercle and body. Atypical ribs are 1, 2, 10, 11 and 12. The sternum has manubrium, body and xiphoid process. The sternal angle, felt where manubrium meets body, lies at the level of the T4/T5 intervertebral disc. It is a key imaging landmark: the aortic arch, tracheal bifurcation and azygos arch lie near this plane.

sections.heading: Intercostal spaces
sections.text: Each intercostal space contains three muscle layers: external, internal and innermost. The intercostal vein, artery and nerve run in the costal groove of the rib above, between the internal and innermost layers. From above downward the order is vein, artery, nerve. For procedures such as thoracentesis, a needle is placed in an intercostal space and kept close to the upper border of the lower rib to avoid this bundle. Local protocols and imaging guidance apply.

sections.heading: Mediastinal divisions
sections.text: The mediastinum is the central compartment between the lungs. A horizontal plane through the sternal angle divides it into superior and inferior parts. The inferior part is divided by the pericardium into anterior, middle and posterior. The superior mediastinum contains the thymus, great vessels, trachea, oesophagus, thoracic duct and phrenic and vagus nerves. The middle mediastinum contains the heart, pericardium, ascending aorta, pulmonary trunk and main bronchi. The posterior mediastinum contains the descending aorta, oesophagus, thoracic duct, azygos vein, vagus nerves and sympathetic trunk.

sections.heading: Diaphragmatic openings
sections.text: The diaphragm has three main openings. The caval opening at T8 transmits the inferior vena cava and right phrenic nerve. The oesophageal opening at T10 transmits the oesophagus and vagal trunks. The aortic opening at T12 transmits the aorta, thoracic duct and azygos vein. Teaching case: Amara in Kano has a pleural effusion. A clinician plans thoracentesis using ultrasound, choosing a space and passing the needle above the lower rib. Check current local guidance before any procedure.

keyPoints: The sternal angle lies at the T4/T5 disc and marks the division between superior and inferior mediastinum.
The intercostal neurovascular bundle runs in the costal groove of the rib above, with vein, artery and nerve from above downward.
The diaphragm openings are caval at T8, oesophageal at T10 and aortic at T12.
The middle mediastinum contains the heart and pericardium; the posterior contains the descending aorta and oesophagus.
For thoracentesis, keep the needle near the upper border of the lower rib and use imaging and local guidance.

en.title: Abdomen and peritoneum
en.short: Abdominal wall, inguinal canal, peritoneum, mesenteries, blood supply and hernias.

sections.heading: Wall and inguinal canal
sections.text: The anterolateral abdominal wall has muscles and fascial layers. The rectus sheath encloses rectus abdominis, and the linea alba is the midline seam. The inguinal canal runs above the medial inguinal ligament. Its deep ring is lateral to the inferior epigastric vessels; its superficial ring is in external oblique aponeurosis. In men the spermatic cord passes through; in women the round ligament. Its floor is the inguinal ligament.

sections.heading: Peritoneum and cavity
sections.text: The peritoneum is a serous membrane. Parietal peritoneum lines the wall; visceral peritoneum covers organs. The peritoneal cavity is a potential space with a thin film of fluid. A mesentery is a double layer of peritoneum that connects an organ to the body wall and carries vessels, nerves and lymphatics. The small intestinal mesentery has a root from the duodenojejunal flexure to the ileocaecal junction. The lesser sac lies behind the stomach and opens into the greater sac through the epiploic foramen.

sections.heading: Visceral relations
sections.text: Intraperitoneal organs are suspended by mesentery and include the liver, stomach, spleen, jejunum, ileum, transverse colon and sigmoid colon. Retroperitoneal organs lie behind the peritoneum and include the kidneys, most of the duodenum, the pancreas except its tail, and the ascending and descending colon. The stomach bed includes the pancreas, spleen, left kidney and transverse colon.

sections.heading: Blood supply and hernias
sections.text: Foregut is supplied by the coeliac trunk, midgut by the superior mesenteric artery and hindgut by the inferior mesenteric artery. The splenic vein joins the superior mesenteric vein behind the pancreatic neck to form the hepatic portal vein, part of the portal system. A hernia is a protrusion through a weak point. An indirect inguinal hernia passes through the deep ring lateral to the inferior epigastric vessels; a direct hernia passes through the posterior wall medial to them. Femoral hernia passes through the femoral canal. For example, a 65-year-old man with a chronic cough develops a direct inguinal hernia.

keyPoints: The inguinal canal’s deep ring lies lateral to the inferior epigastric vessels.
Parietal peritoneum lines the wall; visceral peritoneum covers organs.
A mesentery is a double layer of peritoneum carrying vessels, nerves and lymphatics.
Foregut, midgut and hindgut are supplied by the coeliac trunk, superior mesenteric artery and inferior mesenteric artery.
The hepatic portal vein is formed by the splenic and superior mesenteric veins.
Indirect inguinal hernia is lateral to the inferior epigastric vessels; direct hernia is medial; femoral hernia uses the femoral canal.

en.title: Pelvis and perineum
en.short: Bony pelvis, pelvic floor, perineum, sphincters, pudendal canal and obstetric diameters.

sections.heading: Bony pelvis
sections.text: The bony pelvis is a ring of two hip bones, the sacrum and coccyx. Each hip bone has ilium, ischium and pubis. The pelvic brim divides greater pelvis above from lesser pelvis below. The lesser pelvis has inlet, cavity and outlet. Landmarks include sacral promontory, ischial spine, ischial tuberosity and pubic arch.

sections.heading: Pelvic floor and sphincters
sections.text: The pelvic floor is mainly levator ani (pubococcygeus, puborectalis, iliococcygeus) plus coccygeus. It supports pelvic viscera, resists abdominal pressure and helps continence. Puborectalis slings the anorectal junction. The anal canal has an internal anal sphincter (smooth, involuntary) and an external anal sphincter (skeletal, voluntary, pudendal nerve). The external urethral sphincter is skeletal and voluntary; the internal urethral sphincter, at the bladder neck, is smooth and involuntary and is best developed in males.

sections.heading: Perineum and pudendal canal
sections.text: The perineum is the region below the pelvic floor, bounded by pubic symphysis, ischiopubic rami, ischial tuberosities, sacrotuberous ligaments and coccyx. A line between ischial tuberosities divides it into urogenital triangle anteriorly and anal triangle posteriorly. The anal triangle contains anal canal and ischioanal fossae. The urogenital triangle contains external genitalia and urethra, and in females the vagina. The pudendal canal (Alcock canal) lies in obturator internus fascia on the lateral wall of the ischioanal fossa. It contains internal pudendal vessels and pudendal nerve, supplying perineum and external sphincters.

sections.heading: Viscera and obstetric dimensions
sections.text: In females the bladder is anterior to vagina and uterus; rectum is posterior. In males the prostate lies below bladder and anterior to rectum. Ureters cross the pelvic brim near common iliac bifurcation and pass medially to bladder. Obstetric dimensions describe the inlet. True conjugate: sacral promontory to superior border of pubic symphysis. Obstetric conjugate: to posterior surface of symphysis, not directly measurable clinically. Diagonal conjugate: to inferior border, felt on vaginal examination. Transverse diameter is the widest transverse distance. Values vary by person and population; pelvimetry practice differs by country, so check local guidance.

keyPoints: The bony pelvis is a ring of two hip bones, the sacrum and coccyx; the pelvic brim separates greater and lesser pelvis.
Levator ani and coccygeus form the pelvic floor, supporting viscera and helping continence.
The internal anal sphincter is smooth and involuntary; the external anal sphincter is skeletal, voluntary and supplied by the pudendal nerve.
The perineum is divided into urogenital and anal triangles; the pudendal canal lies in obturator internus fascia and contains the pudendal nerve and internal pudendal vessels.
In females the bladder is anterior to the vagina and uterus; in males the prostate lies below the bladder and anterior to the rectum.
Obstetric conjugates describe the pelvic inlet; the diagonal conjugate can be felt on vaginal examination, but values and pelvimetry practice vary by person and country.

en.title: Head and neck anatomy
en.short: Skull, neck triangles, fascial planes, pharynx, larynx, thyroid, salivary glands, vessels, nerves and airway.

sections.heading: Skull and fossae
sections.text:
The skull has a neurocranium, which encloses the brain, and a viscerocranium, the facial bones. The mandible is the only freely movable bone. Sutures join most skull bones.

The cranial base has three cranial fossae: anterior, middle and posterior. Each fossa holds brain parts and has foramina, openings that transmit nerves and vessels. Facial bones form the orbits, nasal cavity and upper jaw.

sections.heading: Neck triangles and fascia
sections.text:
The sternocleidomastoid muscle divides the neck into an anterior triangle and a posterior triangle. The anterior triangle contains the carotid vessels, thyroid and airway; the posterior contains the brachial plexus and subclavian vessels.

Fascial planes are sheets of connective tissue that separate compartments and allow structures to move. They also form pathways, so infection in the neck can spread along them. The carotid sheath is a fascial tube around the common carotid artery, internal jugular vein and vagus nerve.

sections.heading: Pharynx, larynx and glands
sections.text:
The pharynx is a muscular tube behind the nose and mouth. It has three parts: nasopharynx, oropharynx and laryngopharynx. The larynx is the organ of voice and the upper airway; its cartilages include the thyroid and cricoid.

The thyroid gland lies in front of the trachea and makes thyroid hormones. The major salivary glands are the parotid, submandibular and sublingual glands. The parotid lies in front of the ear; the submandibular is under the jaw; the sublingual is under the tongue. They release saliva through ducts.

sections.heading: Vessels, nerves and airway
sections.text:
The common carotid artery divides into internal and external carotid arteries. The internal jugular vein drains most of the head and neck. The vertebral artery runs in the neck and supplies the brain. Nerves include the cervical plexus, phrenic nerve to the diaphragm, and cranial nerves such as the vagus.

The airway runs from the nasal cavity through the pharynx and larynx to the trachea. Case: Amina has a tooth abscess that spreads along fascial planes, causing neck swelling and airway risk. This shows why dentists and doctors assess swelling, voice and breathing.

keyPoints: The neurocranium encloses the brain; the viscerocranium forms the face.
The cranial base has anterior, middle and posterior fossae with foramina for nerves and vessels.
The sternocleidomastoid divides the neck into anterior and posterior triangles.
Fascial planes separate compartments but can conduct infection.
The pharynx has naso-, oro- and laryngo- parts; the larynx is voice and upper airway.
The carotid sheath contains the common carotid artery, internal jugular vein and vagus nerve.

en.title: Neuroanatomy: brain and spinal cord
en.short: Brain development, cortical areas, deep grey matter, brainstem, cerebellum, spinal tracts, meninges and blood supply.

sections.heading: Development and cortex
sections.text:
The neural tube forms from ectoderm and closes early in pregnancy. Its cranial end becomes five secondary vesicles: telencephalon, diencephalon, mesencephalon, metencephalon and myelencephalon. Failed closure causes neural tube defects; folic acid in early pregnancy lowers risk, following national guidance.

Cortical areas are named by function. The precentral gyrus is primary motor cortex and the postcentral gyrus primary somatosensory cortex. Visual cortex is occipital and auditory cortex temporal. Broca area controls speech production and Wernicke area comprehension, usually on the left.

sections.heading: Deep grey matter
sections.text:
The internal capsule is white matter between thalamus and caudate medially and the lentiform nucleus laterally. It carries ascending sensory and descending motor fibres, so a small infarct can cause opposite-sided weakness or sensory loss.

Basal ganglia are caudate, putamen and globus pallidus plus related nuclei. They modulate movement; damage causes too little movement, as in Parkinsonism, or too much, as in chorea. Thalamus relays most sensory pathways except smell. Hypothalamus controls temperature, hunger, thirst, circadian rhythm and endocrine output.

sections.heading: Brainstem, cord, coverings
sections.text:
The brainstem is midbrain, pons and medulla; it holds cranial nerve nuclei, long tracts and vital centres. The cerebellum coordinates movement, balance and motor learning; lesions cause ataxia and intention tremor, not paralysis.

In the cord, dorsal columns carry fine touch, vibration and proprioception and cross in the medulla. Spinothalamic fibres carry pain and temperature and cross near entry. Corticospinal fibres carry motor commands and cross in the medulla.

Meninges are dura, arachnoid and pia; CSF lies in the subarachnoid space. Ventricles are lateral, third and fourth, with CSF made by choroid plexus and flowing through the aqueduct. Blockage causes hydrocephalus.

sections.heading: Blood supply
sections.text: Blood comes from internal carotid arteries (anterior and middle cerebral) and the vertebral-basilar system (posterior cerebral), linked by the circle of Willis. A left middle cerebral stroke can cause right face and arm weakness with expressive aphasia.

keyPoints: The neural tube gives the brain and spinal cord; failed closure causes neural tube defects, and folic acid in early pregnancy lowers risk.
Precentral and postcentral gyri are primary motor and somatosensory cortex; Broca and Wernicke areas are usually left-sided.
The internal capsule carries sensory and motor fibres, so a small infarct can cause major opposite-sided deficits.
Basal ganglia modulate movement; damage causes too little or too much movement.
Dorsal columns and corticospinal fibres cross in the medulla; spinothalamic fibres cross near cord entry.
CSF flows from lateral to third to fourth ventricle; blockage causes hydrocephalus.

en.title: Cranial nerves
en.short: The twelve cranial nerves: nuclei, course, branches, functions and the anatomy behind testing them.

sections.heading: Organisation
sections.text: Cranial nerves are twelve paired nerves that leave the brain and brainstem through bony foramina (openings) in the skull. They carry functional types: motor to skeletal muscle, sensory from skin and organs, special sensory (smell, vision, hearing, balance, taste), and parasympathetic secretomotor fibres. Their nuclei, groups of neuron cell bodies, lie in the brainstem, except olfactory and optic, which connect to the forebrain. Motor and sensory nuclei are arranged in columns; parasympathetic nuclei belong to III, VII, IX and X.

sections.heading: The twelve nerves
sections.text:
I Olfactory: smell.
II Optic: vision.
III Oculomotor: most extraocular muscles, eyelid, pupil constriction, lens shape.
IV Trochlear: superior oblique.
V Trigeminal: face sensation, mastication.
VI Abducens: lateral rectus.
VII Facial: facial expression, taste from anterior tongue, lacrimal and salivary secretion.
VIII Vestibulocochlear: hearing and balance.
IX Glossopharyngeal: taste from posterior tongue, pharynx, carotid body and sinus, parotid secretion.
X Vagus: pharynx and larynx, thoracic and abdominal viscera.
XI Accessory: sternocleidomastoid and trapezius; its cranial root joins X.
XII Hypoglossal: tongue muscles.

sections.heading: Course and branches
sections.text: Each nerve follows a characteristic route. I passes through the cribriform plate; II through the optic canal; III, IV, V1 and VI through the superior orbital fissure; V2 through foramen rotundum; V3 through foramen ovale; VII and VIII through the internal acoustic meatus; IX, X and XI through the jugular foramen; XII through the hypoglossal canal. V divides into ophthalmic, maxillary and mandibular branches. VII divides into temporal, zygomatic, buccal, marginal mandibular and cervical branches. IX gives pharyngeal branches; X gives pharyngeal and laryngeal branches.

sections.heading: Testing and localisation
sections.text: Test by function: I smell; II acuity; III, IV, VI eye movements and pupil; V face sensation, jaw; VII expression, taste; VIII hearing, balance; IX, X palate and gag; XI shrug, head turn; XII tongue. Lower motor neuron facial lesions weaken the whole side; upper motor neuron lesions spare the forehead because the upper face has bilateral cortical input. Amina has right facial weakness with a smooth forehead, suggesting a right facial nerve lesion.

keyPoints: Cranial nerves are numbered I to XII and may carry motor, sensory, special sensory or parasympathetic fibres.
Most cranial nerve nuclei lie in the brainstem; I and II connect to the forebrain.
Each nerve exits through a named skull foramen, which helps localise lesions.
V has three divisions; VII has five main facial branches.
Test each nerve by the function it supplies; forehead sparing separates upper from lower motor neuron facial lesions.
XI’s spinal root supplies sternocleidomastoid and trapezius; its cranial root joins X.

en.title: Autonomic nervous system: visceral control and referred pain
en.short: Sympathetic and parasympathetic divisions, ganglia, plexuses, enteric system, visceral innervation and referred pain.

sections.heading: Divisions and outflow
sections.text: The autonomic nervous system (ANS) controls smooth muscle, cardiac muscle and glands. Its sympathetic division has thoracolumbar outflow from T1 to L2. Preganglionic fibres are short, synapsing in paravertebral or prevertebral ganglia; postganglionic fibres are long. The adrenal medulla is an exception with direct preganglionic supply. The parasympathetic division has craniosacral outflow through cranial nerves III, VII, IX and X and sacral segments S2 to S4. Its preganglionic fibres are long and its ganglia lie near or inside the target organ, so postganglionic fibres are short. Most organs receive both divisions.

sections.heading: Ganglia and plexuses
sections.text: A ganglion is a cluster of neuron cell bodies outside the central nervous system. Sympathetic ganglia include the paravertebral chain and prevertebral ganglia such as the coeliac and mesenteric ganglia. A plexus is a network of nerves and ganglia around vessels or organs, such as cardiac and coeliac plexuses. These plexuses carry sympathetic, parasympathetic and visceral afferent fibres. The enteric nervous system is the intrinsic nerve network of the gut wall. Its myenteric (Auerbach) plexus controls motility between the muscle layers; the submucosal (Meissner) plexus controls secretion and blood flow. It can act locally but is modulated by both divisions.

sections.heading: Visceral innervation and referred pain
sections.text: Viscera receive autonomic motor fibres and visceral afferents, sensory fibres travelling with autonomic nerves. Most abdominal visceral afferents follow sympathetic nerves; pelvic ones follow parasympathetic nerves. Visceral pain is vague, midline and accompanied by nausea or sweating, because afferents are few and enter the spinal cord at several levels. Referred pain occurs when visceral afferents enter the cord at the same segment as somatic afferents from the skin; the brain misattributes the pain to that skin area. Amina has early appendicitis: stretch of the appendix sends afferents to T10, so she feels pain around the umbilicus. Later, inflammation reaches the parietal peritoneum, which is somatic, and pain becomes sharp in the right iliac fossa. Cardiac ischaemia can refer pain to the left arm and neck through T1 to T5.

keyPoints: Sympathetic outflow is thoracolumbar (T1 to L2) with short preganglionic and long postganglionic fibres.
Parasympathetic outflow is craniosacral (cranial nerves III, VII, IX and X; S2 to S4) with long preganglionic and short postganglionic fibres.
Prevertebral ganglia and autonomic plexuses distribute fibres, and the enteric plexuses control gut motility and secretion.
Visceral afferents travel with autonomic nerves; most abdominal ones follow sympathetic nerves and pelvic ones follow parasympathetic nerves.
Referred pain occurs when visceral and somatic afferents converge on the same spinal segment, so the brain projects the pain to skin.
Early appendicitis classically causes umbilical pain at T10 before parietal peritoneal inflammation localises it to the right iliac fossa.

en.title: Special senses
en.short: Eye, orbit, extraocular muscles, ear, hearing, balance, taste and smell.

sections.heading: Eye and orbit
sections.text: The eye lies in the bony orbit, a cone-shaped space of several skull bones. The eyeball has three coats: fibrous sclera and cornea, vascular uvea (choroid, ciliary body, iris), and neural retina. Cornea and lens refract light; the iris controls pupil size. The optic nerve (CN II) leaves through the optic canal. Lacrimal gland, fat and vessels fill the orbit.

sections.heading: Extraocular muscles
sections.text: Six extraocular muscles move each eye: four recti and two obliques. Medial rectus turns the eye inward; lateral rectus outward. Superior rectus elevates; inferior rectus depresses. Obliques mainly rotate the eye. CN III supplies all except lateral rectus (CN VI) and superior oblique (CN IV). Case: Aminu has double vision looking right, and his right eye cannot turn outward, suggesting right CN VI weakness.

sections.heading: Ear and balance
sections.text: The ear has external, middle and inner parts. The external ear collects sound. The middle ear has the tympanic membrane and three ossicles (malleus, incus, stapes), which pass sound inward; the Eustachian tube balances pressure. The cochlea serves hearing, and the vestibular apparatus serves balance. Cochlear hair cells convert sound to nerve signals carried by CN VIII, which also carries balance signals. Semicircular canals detect head rotation; utricle and saccule detect gravity and linear acceleration. One-sided damage can cause vertigo and nystagmus.

sections.heading: Taste and smell
sections.text: Taste buds lie mainly on the tongue and are supplied by CN VII, IX and X. They detect sweet, salty, sour, bitter and umami. Smell comes from olfactory epithelium in the roof of the nasal cavity; axons pass through the cribriform plate as CN I. Smell and taste both depend on dissolved chemicals. Loss of smell after head injury suggests shearing of olfactory fibres. Case: a market worker loses smell after a fall; flavour is dulled, because it depends on both senses.

keyPoints: The eyeball has fibrous, vascular and neural coats, and the optic nerve leaves through the optic canal.
CN III supplies most extraocular muscles; lateral rectus is CN VI and superior oblique is CN IV.
The middle ear ossicles are malleus, incus and stapes, and the Eustachian tube balances pressure.
Cochlear hair cells convert sound to signals carried in CN VIII, while semicircular canals and the utricle and saccule detect rotation and linear acceleration.
Taste buds use CN VII, IX and X and detect sweet, salty, sour, bitter and umami.
Olfactory axons pass through the cribriform plate as CN I, and smell contributes to flavour.

en.title: Endocrine system anatomy
en.short: Pituitary, thyroid, parathyroid, adrenal, pancreatic islets, gonads and pineal: relations, blood supply, development.

sections.heading: Pituitary and pineal
sections.text: The pituitary lies in the sella turcica below the optic chiasm, joined to the hypothalamus by the infundibulum. The anterior lobe develops from Rathke pouch, an ectodermal mouth upgrowth; the posterior lobe from the diencephalon. The anterior lobe receives superior hypophyseal arteries and portal blood; the posterior lobe, inferior hypophyseal arteries. The pineal gland sits on the third ventricle roof, develops from neuroectoderm, and is supplied by posterior cerebral and choroidal arteries.

sections.heading: Thyroid and parathyroid
sections.text: The thyroid lies in the anterior neck in front of the trachea. It develops from an endodermal pharyngeal downgrowth and descends along the thyroglossal duct. Its blood supply is the superior thyroid artery from the external carotid and the inferior thyroid artery from the thyrocervical trunk. Parathyroids usually lie on the posterior thyroid surface. The superior pair develops from the fourth pharyngeal pouch; the inferior pair from the third, with the thymus. They are supplied mainly by inferior thyroid arteries. In thyroidectomy, the recurrent laryngeal nerve lies near the inferior thyroid artery.

sections.heading: Adrenal glands
sections.text: The adrenal glands are retroperitoneal on the upper kidney poles. The cortex develops from intermediate mesoderm; the medulla from neural crest. They receive superior suprarenal arteries from the inferior phrenic artery, middle suprarenal arteries from the aorta, and inferior suprarenal arteries from the renal artery. The right suprarenal vein drains to the inferior vena cava; the left to the left renal vein. The right gland lies near the inferior vena cava and liver; the left near the spleen and pancreas.

sections.heading: Pancreatic islets and gonads
sections.text: Pancreatic islets are endocrine cell clusters in the retroperitoneal pancreas behind the stomach. They develop from foregut endoderm and are supplied by pancreatic branches of splenic, superior mesenteric and gastroduodenal arteries. The gonads develop from intermediate mesoderm and coelomic epithelium. Ovaries lie in the pelvis and testes in the scrotum. Gonadal arteries arise from the aorta; the right gonadal vein drains to the inferior vena cava, the left to the left renal vein.

keyPoints: The pituitary anterior lobe arises from Rathke pouch and the posterior lobe from the diencephalon.
The thyroid arises from pharyngeal endoderm and receives superior and inferior thyroid arteries.
Superior parathyroids arise from the fourth pharyngeal pouch and inferior parathyroids from the third.
The adrenal cortex is mesodermal and the medulla is neural crest; three suprarenal arterial sources supply them.
Pancreatic islets are endodermal, while gonads arise from intermediate mesoderm and coelomic epithelium.
The pineal gland is neuroectodermal and lies on the roof of the third ventricle.

en.title: Lymphatic system and immune anatomy
en.short: Lymph vessels, nodes, ducts, spleen, thymus, tonsils, MALT and regional drainage.

sections.heading: Vessels and ducts
sections.text: Lymph is tissue fluid that enters blind-ended lymph capillaries. These capillaries are more permeable than blood capillaries and are absent from the central nervous system and a few other tissues. Collecting vessels contain valves and pass through lymph nodes. Lymph trunks join to form two ducts. The thoracic duct drains the whole body except the right side of the head and neck, the right upper limb and the right thorax. Those regions drain through the right lymphatic duct into the venous system.

sections.heading: Nodes and drainage
sections.text: Lymph nodes are bean-shaped filters. Afferent vessels enter the convex surface and efferent vessels leave the hilum. The cortex contains B-cell follicles, the paracortex contains T cells, and the medulla contains macrophages and plasma cells. Nodes trap microbes and cancer cells and start immune responses. Regional drainage follows the body region: cervical nodes drain the head and neck, axillary nodes the upper limb and breast, inguinal nodes the lower limb and perineum, and mesenteric nodes the gut.

sections.heading: Spleen and thymus
sections.text: The spleen lies in the left upper abdomen. It is the largest lymphoid organ. White pulp around its arteries contains lymphocytes, while red pulp removes old red blood cells and stores platelets. The spleen filters blood, not lymph. The thymus lies in the anterior superior mediastinum. It is large in children and shrinks after puberty. T lymphocytes mature there and learn to tolerate the body’s own tissues.

sections.heading: Tonsils and MALT
sections.text: Tonsils are lymphoid tissue guarding the entrance to the pharynx. The palatine, lingual, pharyngeal and tubal tonsils form Waldeyer’s ring. Mucosa-associated lymphoid tissue, or MALT, protects other mucosal surfaces. Gut-associated lymphoid tissue includes Peyer’s patches and the appendix; bronchial-associated lymphoid tissue lies in the airways. In practice, drainage explains signs: a breast cancer may spread first to axillary nodes, and an infected foot may cause tender inguinal nodes.

keyPoints: Lymph capillaries are blind-ended and drain tissue fluid; collecting vessels have valves and pass through nodes.
The thoracic duct drains most of the body; the right lymphatic duct drains the right head, neck, upper limb and thorax.
Lymph nodes filter lymph and contain B-cell follicles, T-cell paracortex and medullary macrophages.
Regional nodes include cervical, axillary, inguinal and mesenteric groups.
The spleen filters blood and the thymus matures T cells.
Tonsils and MALT guard mucosal surfaces, including Waldeyer’s ring and Peyer’s patches.

en.title: Integumentary system anatomy
en.short: Skin layers, appendages, subcutaneous tissue, fascia, vessels, nerves and regional differences.

sections.heading: Skin layers
sections.text: The skin has two main layers. The epidermis is avascular stratified squamous epithelium; its outer stratum corneum is keratinised and waterproof. The dermis is connective tissue with collagen and elastin, containing vessels, nerves and appendages. Below is the hypodermis, or subcutaneous tissue, mainly loose connective tissue and fat. It binds skin to underlying structures and stores energy. The term superficial fascia is often used for this fatty layer, while deep fascia is dense connective tissue that wraps muscles.

sections.heading: Appendages and fat
sections.text: Appendages are structures derived from epidermis: hair follicles, nails, sweat glands and sebaceous glands. Eccrine sweat glands open onto skin and help thermoregulation; apocrine glands open into hair follicles and become active at puberty. Sebaceous glands secrete sebum into hair follicles. Nails protect fingertips. Subcutaneous fat varies with sex, age, nutrition and site, and it insulates and cushions.

sections.heading: Fascia, vessels and nerves
sections.text: Blood reaches skin through dermal plexuses fed by perforating branches from underlying vessels. The epidermis has no vessels and is nourished by diffusion from the dermis. Cutaneous nerves carry sensation from receptors for touch, temperature, pain and pressure. Each spinal nerve supplies a dermatome, a band of skin. Overlap means damage to one nerve may not cause complete numbness.

sections.heading: Regional variation
sections.text: Regional variation is marked. Skin is thick and hairless on palms and soles, thin and hairy elsewhere. It is mobile over joints and tightly bound over the shin. In a case, a farmer in Ghana has a cut on the shin: little subcutaneous tissue and firm deep fascia limit swelling, while eyelid skin is loose and swells easily. Such differences guide wound care and flap design.

keyPoints: The epidermis is avascular keratinised epithelium; the dermis contains vessels, nerves and appendages.
The hypodermis is mainly fat and loose connective tissue, often called superficial fascia, while deep fascia wraps muscles.
Skin appendages include hair follicles, nails, sweat glands and sebaceous glands.
Dermal plexuses supply the skin, and the epidermis is nourished by diffusion.
Cutaneous nerves carry sensation, and each spinal nerve supplies a dermatome with overlap.
Skin thickness, hairiness, mobility and fat vary by region, which affects swelling and wound behaviour.

en.title: Radiological and sectional anatomy
en.short: Planes, viewing conventions and normal cross-sectional anatomy on X-ray, CT, MRI and ultrasound.

sections.heading: Planes and orientation
sections.text: Sectional imaging shows the body in slices. The axial (transverse) plane is horizontal and separates superior from inferior. The coronal plane is vertical and separates anterior from posterior. The sagittal plane is vertical and separates left from right; the midsagittal plane lies in the midline. Axial images are viewed as if from the patient’s feet, so the patient’s right appears on the viewer’s left. Coronal images are viewed as if facing the patient. Sagittal images are viewed from the side. Check side markers.

sections.heading: Radiographs and CT
sections.text: A plain radiograph is a two-dimensional projection made with X-rays. Dense structures absorb more X-rays and look white: bone and metal. Air looks black, fat dark grey and soft tissue grey. Overlap means two views are often needed. A chest radiograph is commonly posteroanterior (PA) and is viewed as if facing the patient, so the patient’s right lung is on the viewer’s left. Computed tomography (CT) uses X-rays from many angles to reconstruct axial slices, which can be reformatted into coronal and sagittal images. CT shows bone well and uses Hounsfield units: water is 0, air about −1000 and bone about +1000.

sections.heading: MRI, ultrasound and regions
sections.text: Magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) uses a strong magnetic field and radiofrequency pulses, not ionising radiation, and gives excellent soft-tissue contrast. Ultrasound uses high-frequency sound waves and a probe; it is operator dependent and limited by bone and gas. In the thorax, the lungs surround the heart and mediastinum. In the abdomen, the liver lies on the patient’s right, the spleen on the left, the kidneys posteriorly, the aorta left of the spine and the inferior vena cava to its right. In the pelvis, a midline sagittal view shows the bladder anteriorly and the rectum posteriorly; the uterus lies between them in a female, and the prostate in a male. On an axial abdominal CT viewed from the feet, the liver appears on the viewer’s left because it is on the patient’s right.

keyPoints: Axial, coronal and sagittal planes are standard sectional planes; axial separates superior from inferior.
Axial images are viewed from the patient’s feet, so the patient’s right is on the viewer’s left.
Plain radiographs are two-dimensional projections; air is black, fat dark grey, soft tissue grey and bone white.
CT uses X-rays and Hounsfield units; MRI uses magnetic fields and radiofrequency pulses without ionising radiation.
Ultrasound is real-time and avoids ionising radiation but is operator dependent and limited by bone and gas.
In normal cross-sectional anatomy, the liver is on the patient’s right and the spleen on the left; check side markers.

en.title: Surface anatomy and clinical examination
en.short: Surface landmarks and the anatomy behind palpation, percussion, auscultation and safe procedures.

sections.heading: Landmarks and planes
sections.text: Surface anatomy links visible or palpable features to deeper structures. It uses standard planes and lines, such as the median sagittal plane, midclavicular line and transpyloric plane, to describe where organs and vessels lie. A landmark is reliable only when it is consistent and easy to find. The sternal angle is a useful example: it lies where the second costal cartilage joins the sternum, near the T4/T5 intervertebral disc. From it, a clinician can count ribs and intercostal spaces. Other landmarks include the anterior superior iliac spine and pubic symphysis. Compare both sides and note body build, because obesity, pregnancy and deformity change what can be felt.

sections.heading: Palpation and percussion
sections.text: Palpation is examination by touch. Light palpation detects tenderness and temperature; deep palpation feels organs and masses. The hands are placed so the palms or fingertips follow the shape of the structure. Percussion is tapping a finger against the body to judge the density of tissue beneath. Air-filled lung is resonant, solid liver is dull, and gas in the stomach is tympanic. These sounds depend on the thickness of the chest or abdominal wall, so percussion is one part of the examination.
