In a volunteer, percussion over the right lower chest is dull because the liver lies under the diaphragm, while over the stomach on the left the note may be tympanic because of gas.

sections.heading: Auscultation and safety
sections.text: Auscultation is listening with a stethoscope. It works because sound travels through tissues and is altered by air, fluid or solid. Heart sounds are best heard at chest wall sites where each valve’s sound is carried by blood flow; these sites are named after the valves but are not exactly where the valves project. Breath sounds are heard over the lungs. Safe procedures use the same landmarks: the clinician identifies layers, avoids nerves and vessels, and checks the site before inserting a needle or cannula. For example, in the cubital fossa the median cubital vein is superficial, while the brachial artery and median nerve lie deeper. Procedure guidelines differ by country and change, so follow current national or WHO guidance and local policy.

keyPoints: Surface landmarks relate palpable or visible features to deeper structures and are useful only when consistent.
Palpation uses light and deep touch to detect tenderness, temperature, organs and masses.
Percussion is resonant over air, dull over solid tissue and tympanic over gas.
Auscultation depends on where sounds are generated and how they are transmitted to the chest wall.
Safe procedures use landmarks to identify layers and avoid nerves and vessels.
Procedure guidelines differ by country and change, so check current national or WHO guidance and local policy.

en.title: Anatomy ethics and body donation
en.short: Consent, respect, confidentiality and law in cadaver dissection and body donation.

sections.heading: Consent and donation
sections.text: Body donation is the voluntary gift of a whole body after death for anatomy teaching or research. Valid consent must be informed, voluntary and given by someone with capacity; the donor should understand the purpose, what will happen, and the right to withdraw before death. Some countries require the donor’s own consent, some also require family authorisation, and some allow either. The law varies by country. In England, Wales and Northern Ireland the Human Tissue Act 2004 governs consent; Scotland has the Human Tissue (Scotland) Act 2006. In Nigeria, check the National Health Act 2014 and your school’s rules. Never assume an unclaimed body may be used: unclaimed bodies are ethically contested and rules differ.

sections.heading: Respect and confidentiality
sections.text: A cadaver was once a living person, and many were donors; it is not an object. Handle the body with dignity: keep it covered when not being studied, use gloves, and avoid unnecessary exposure. Do not take photographs or videos, and never post images on social media. Keep the donor’s identity and medical details confidential; discuss the body only for learning. Respect cultural and religious beliefs, and follow the law and the donor’s wishes for final disposal, such as burial or cremation. Professional behaviour includes punctuality, preparation, quiet speech, no food or drink, and no jokes. These habits show respect and protect the trust that makes donation possible.

sections.heading: Law and case
sections.text:
Law sets who may consent, how records are kept, how bodies are transported and disposed of, and whether money may change hands. Sale of bodies or tissue is prohibited in many countries; check yours. An anatomy ethics committee or licensed facility usually oversees donation and use. This is education, not legal advice.

Case: Ngozi, a final-year student in Enugu, Nigeria, sees Tunde filming a cadaver for social media. She should stop him, tell the demonstrator, and report to the anatomy committee. The images must be deleted. The breach is serious because it breaks confidentiality and dignity, and it can damage public trust in body donation.

keyPoints: Body donation is a voluntary gift for anatomy teaching or research, and valid consent must be informed, voluntary and revocable before death.
The law on consent, family authorisation, unclaimed bodies and disposal varies by country, so check national law and your school’s rules or anatomy committee.
Treat every cadaver with dignity: keep it covered, use gloves and avoid unnecessary exposure.
Never photograph or share cadaver images, and keep the donor’s identity and medical details confidential.
Unclaimed bodies are not automatically available for dissection; their use is ethically contested and legally restricted in many places.
Professional behaviour in the dissection room includes punctuality, preparation, quiet speech and no food, drink or jokes.

en.title: Advanced neuroanatomy
en.short: Functional systems, cortical networks, imaging anatomy and disease mechanisms in the nervous system.

sections.heading: Systems and pathways
sections.text: Functional neural systems are groups of neurons linked by pathways that serve a function, such as vision, movement, language or memory. A pathway is a set of axons with a common origin and destination. Cortical regions are not isolated; white matter tracts connect them. For example, the hippocampus helps form new declarative memories, while the basal ganglia help select movement. Damage to a pathway can cause a deficit even when its cortical endpoints look normal.

sections.heading: Cortical networks
sections.text: Cortical networks are distributed sets of regions that cooperate. The connectome is the full map of anatomical connections. Functional imaging describes networks by correlated activity, not proof of causation. Commonly described networks include the default mode network, active at rest and suppressed during focused tasks; the salience network, which flags important stimuli; and executive networks for working memory. These labels are useful models, not fixed boxes. A hub is a highly connected node, so hub damage can disturb many functions.

sections.heading: Imaging anatomy
sections.text: Neuroimaging shows anatomy in vivo. CT is fast and shows bone and acute blood. MRI gives better soft tissue contrast: T1-weighted images show anatomy, T2-weighted and fluid-attenuated images show pathology such as oedema, and diffusion-weighted imaging shows restricted diffusion in acute infarction. Diffusion tensor imaging maps white matter tracts. Functional MRI measures blood oxygen level dependent signal, an indirect marker of activity. In axial images, radiological convention places the patient’s left on the right side of the image.

sections.heading: Disease basis
sections.text: Neurological disease reflects damage to a node or its connections. A left middle cerebral artery infarct in a right-handed person causes right face and arm weakness and aphasia, because it damages left motor cortex and language networks. Multiple sclerosis plaques in white matter interrupt tracts. Parkinson disease involves loss of dopaminergic neurons in the substantia nigra pars compacta. Alzheimer disease begins in medial temporal and hippocampal regions. Epilepsy reflects abnormal synchronous activity in a network. Check current national or WHO guidance for imaging and treatment.

keyPoints: Functional systems are defined by connected pathways, not by single cortical spots.
The connectome maps anatomical connections; functional networks are inferred from correlated activity.
Hub damage can cause widespread deficits because hubs connect many regions.
CT shows bone and acute blood; MRI sequences show different tissues and pathology.
A left middle cerebral artery infarct can cause right face and arm weakness and aphasia.
Parkinson disease involves substantia nigra dopaminergic loss; Alzheimer disease begins in medial temporal regions.

en.title: Advanced developmental anatomy
en.short: Molecular signals, teratogens, congenital anomalies and developmental origins of variation.

sections.heading: Signals and genes
sections.text:
Organogenesis is organ formation from three germ layers. It depends on signalling between cells. Conserved pathways include Hedgehog, Wnt, BMP, FGF and Notch. They set boundaries, control proliferation and death, and specify cell fate. Hox genes give positional identity along the body axis.

Epithelial-mesenchymal transition (EMT) lets epithelial cells loosen and migrate. Neural crest cells use EMT to leave the neural tube and form peripheral neurons, melanocytes and facial tissues. Apoptosis, programmed cell death, sculpts spaces and separates digits. Disruption of any step can cause a structural anomaly.

sections.heading: Teratogens and anomalies
sections.text:
A teratogen is an agent that causes a congenital anomaly after exposure of the embryo or fetus. Its effect depends on dose, timing, genotype and species. The embryonic period, weeks three to eight, is the main critical period for major structural defects. Later exposure mainly affects growth and function.

Examples include alcohol, which causes fetal alcohol spectrum disorder, and rubella virus, which can cause cataracts, deafness and cardiac defects after early infection. Thalidomide caused limb defects such as phocomelia.

Anomalies are classified as malformation (abnormal formation), disruption (damage to normal tissue), deformation (mechanical distortion) and dysplasia (abnormal tissue organisation). A sequence is a chain of consequences from one primary defect; a syndrome is a recognised pattern of several anomalies with a single cause, such as a gene or chromosome change.

sections.heading: Variation and origins
sections.text:
Normal anatomy varies. Variation arises during development: incomplete regression, altered fusion, differences in vessel branching and left-right asymmetry. Some variants are harmless; others raise clinical risk. A persistent left superior vena cava may complicate central line placement.

The developmental origins of health and disease (DOHaD) hypothesis proposes that conditions before birth and in early life influence later disease risk. Epigenetic marks, such as DNA methylation, may mediate this. Evidence is strongest in epidemiology and animal models; mechanisms vary, so avoid overclaiming.

A child with a ventricular septal defect may have it as an isolated malformation, or the defect may be part of a syndrome. Population differences in anomaly rates reflect reporting, consanguinity, infection and environment, not one universal cause.

keyPoints: Organogenesis depends on conserved signalling pathways such as Hedgehog, Wnt, BMP, FGF and Notch.
Hox genes give positional identity, and EMT allows neural crest cells to migrate.
Teratogen effects depend on dose, timing, genotype and species; the embryonic period is the main critical period for major structural defects.
Anomalies are classified as malformation, disruption, deformation and dysplasia; a sequence follows one primary defect, while a syndrome is a pattern of several anomalies with a single cause.
Normal anatomical variation often reflects incomplete regression, altered fusion or asymmetric development.
The DOHaD hypothesis links early-life conditions to later disease risk, partly through epigenetic marks, but mechanisms vary.

en.title: Anatomical research methods: dissection, measurement and imaging
en.short: How anatomical studies are designed: dissection, morphometry, imaging, statistics, ethics and writing.

sections.heading: Dissection and morphometry
sections.text:
Dissection-based research uses cadavers or prosections (pre-dissected specimens) to study structure. A research dissection follows a written protocol: specimen number, preservation method, dissection steps and photographed landmarks. Record what you see before you interpret it.

Morphometry is the measurement of shape and size. Define each landmark, use calibrated callipers or a digitizer, and repeat measurements to estimate observer error. For example, if femoral head diameters in five dry bones are 44, 46, 45, 47 and 48 mm, the mean is (44+46+45+47+48) ÷ 5 = 230 ÷ 5 = 46 mm. The range is 44 to 48 mm. Report units and specimen numbers.

sections.heading: Imaging and measurement error
sections.text:
Imaging methods include radiography, computed tomography (CT), magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) and ultrasound. They allow living anatomy and three-dimensional models. Segmentation means outlining a structure on each image slice; it depends on contrast, slice thickness and the observer. State the scanner, settings and software.

Radiation dose matters for CT, so justify it. Measurement error can be assessed by repeating scans or measurements and reporting agreement, such as the intraclass correlation coefficient (ICC), where values near 1 mean strong agreement.

sections.heading: Statistics and ethics
sections.text:
Statistics turns observations into evidence. Describe the sample, then choose tests that match the design. A sample size calculation needs an expected difference, a measure of variability and a chosen error rate; use a statistician early.

Ethics approval comes before data collection. An ethics committee reviews consent, confidentiality and body donation rules. These rules differ by country, so check current national guidance and your institution’s policy. Anonymise images and store data securely.

sections.heading: Dissertation writing
sections.text:
Dissertation writing follows a clear structure: introduction, methods, results and discussion. The methods section must let another researcher repeat the study. Report landmarks, equipment, inclusion criteria and statistical tests.

In the discussion, compare with published work and state limitations honestly. Cite primary sources and follow your department’s style. A good anatomy dissertation is reproducible, ethical and modest about what the data can show.

keyPoints: Dissection research needs a written protocol and photographed landmarks.
Morphometry requires defined landmarks, calibrated tools and repeat measurements.
Mean = sum of values ÷ number of values; report units and sample size.
Imaging studies must state scanner, settings, segmentation method and radiation justification.
Ethics approval and local body donation rules come before data collection.
A dissertation methods section must be reproducible and limitations stated honestly.

en.title: Computational and imaging anatomy
en.short: Segmentation, 3D reconstruction, morphometry and computational models, with their limits.

sections.heading: Segmentation
sections.text:
Segmentation labels each pixel in a 2D image or each voxel in a 3D image as belonging to a structure. A voxel is a small volume element, the 3D equivalent of a pixel.

Methods include manual tracing, intensity thresholding, atlas-based methods using a reference anatomy, and machine learning. Manual tracing varies between observers. Automatic methods can fail with low contrast, artefact or unusual anatomy. The result is a label map, not a measurement, until checked.

sections.heading: Three-dimensional reconstruction
sections.text:
Three-dimensional reconstruction turns a stack of segmented images into a visible model. Surface rendering creates a mesh of triangles around the boundary, often by a standard algorithm called marching cubes. Volume rendering shows the whole volume with different opacity.

Reconstruction depends on slice thickness and spacing. Gaps between slices are interpolated, which can smooth or invent detail. A model is an interpretation, not a photograph of the body.

sections.heading: Morphometry and models
sections.text:
Morphometry is the measurement of shape and size. Common measures are volume, surface area, length, thickness and curvature, often from landmarks, which are defined points. Computational models include finite element models, which divide a structure into small elements to calculate stress or strain, and statistical shape models, which describe variation around a mean shape. They need assumptions about tissue properties and boundary conditions, meaning what happens at the edges of the model.

For example, voxels of 0.5 mm × 0.5 mm × 1.0 mm have a volume of 0.25 mm³. If a structure contains 40,000 such voxels, its volume is 40,000 × 0.25 = 10,000 mm³, or 10 cm³, because 1 cm³ = 1,000 mm³. Partial volume at the edges can bias this figure.

sections.heading: Limits and validation
sections.text:
Limitations accumulate. Resolution, noise, motion and metal artefact affect segmentation. Partial volume mixes tissues within one voxel. Registration, which aligns images from different times or modalities, can add error.

Results vary with software and observer. Validation against phantoms (test objects that mimic tissue), dissection or expert labels is essential. Computational anatomy supports research and surgical planning, but does not replace clinical judgement. Patient images are personal data, so consent and data protection rules apply.

keyPoints: Segmentation assigns labels to pixels or voxels and must be validated before measurement.
Surface and volume rendering build 3D models from image stacks, with interpolation that can add or smooth detail.
Morphometry measures volume, surface area, length, thickness and curvature, often from landmarks.
Voxel volume = x spacing × y spacing × z spacing; for 0.5 × 0.5 × 1.0 mm it is 0.25 mm³.
Finite element and statistical shape models depend on assumptions and on the data used to build them.
Image resolution, partial volume, registration error and observer variation limit every computational result.
